6.4 — Double Jump: Boots or Potion

The potion from 2.3 raised a number that already had a ceiling. This pickup changes something else entirely: it changes what your level design is allowed to ask for. And it comes in two flavours, which are genuinely different games. Boots raise your jump allowance for the rest of the run — every gap in the cave is yours to widen. A potion raises it for a few seconds and then takes it back — the cave stays the same size, and you get to cross the part of it you could not. Pick one, build it, and be ready to say why the other one is worse for your game.

Either way, the machinery is already in your file. 6.2 left you with a budget — jumpsRemaining, maxJumps, a refill on the ground, and a charge for walking off a ledge. Today changes one of those fields. And the walk-off rule pays off for free: a player carrying boots who steps off a ledge is charged one jump, keeps the other. That is the difference between a double jump and a jetpack, and you already built it.

Search terms for this lesson“in unity how to make a double jump, how to make a temporary power up that wears off, how to count the jumps a player has left”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

Tap the key in mid-air and jump a second time — but only after you have picked something up. The budget you wrote in 6.2 already counts jumps and already knows how many you are allowed; what it has never had is a reason for that number to be anything but one. So this lesson is not a new mechanic. It is one field changing — and a decision about whether it ever changes back.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Raise the ceiling, not the countwhat does this part do?Read: 6.2 — Ground Checks: No Infinite Jumps: the two fields in the class body, the refill, and the charge for walking off
  2. Decide whether the fact is permanent or temporarywhat does this part do?Read: 2.3 — Healing Pickups & the Max-Health Cap, for the pickup that moves a ceiling rather than filling a number
  3. Build the pickup that does itwhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat (tag, trigger, callback, destroy) and 2.3 for the second pickup
  4. Give the temporary version a clockwhat does this part do?Read: 3.3 — Fire Rate: Cooldowns & Time: the countdown, and Time.deltaTime as the unit of "one second of play"
  5. Decide what happens the frame it runs outwhat does this part do?Read: the refill and the charge in 6.2, which are the only two other places the budget is written
  6. Put the pickup where the level can ask for itwhat does this part do?Read: the prefab-versus-instance rule and the placement work in 2.1, and the playtest habits from 2.4
  7. Say what happens to it when you diewhat does this part do?Read: 2.7 — Refactor Day: Moving Stats into the StatManager, and 5.3 for the object that survives a scene load

Six of those seven parts are things you have already built, and the seventh is a decision. What is genuinely new is small enough to miss: a capability has a lifetime, and you get to choose it. Permanent and temporary are not two ways of writing the same feature — they change what your level can ask for. The boots rewrite every gap in the cave, forever. The potion rewrites the gaps you can reach in the next few seconds, and then the level snaps back. The code is one field either way; the choice is the work.

The test for a finished split: does the part name something you could point at — a field, a line, a branch, an object in the Hierarchy? "Make a double jump" points at nothing. "Where the counter goes back down when the clock runs out" points at one branch, and that is a part.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Boots raise a ceiling and never lower it; a potion opens a window and then closes it. Neither one is written in fewer lines than the other — say what a player learns from each, and which lesson your cave is trying to teach.

There is exactly one moment in the whole game where the count should go back up, and 6.2 already put it there. Name it — then say what the temporary version has to add that the permanent version never does.

In the Editor ~25 min
  1. On paper, in one sentence: boots or potion, and what the other one would have cost you. Write it in your notebook where you can read it back at the end of the period — the checkpoint asks you to defend it, and the editor steps below branch on it.
  2. Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers → add the tag you need: Boots, or something like JumpPotion. Read the list while you are in there: it ships six tags and every one is a name somebody has to remember. If your healing pickup from 2.3 already answers to Potion, your jump potion needs its own name — one tag cannot mean two different things.
  3. Hierarchy → right-click → 2D Object → Sprites → Square, and rename it. Then Project window → Assets/Artwork, pick a sprite you are not using, and drop it into Inspector → Sprite Renderer → Sprite. There is no boots art anywhere in this project — no file matching boot, no prefab — so tint it with Sprite Renderer → Color until it could not be mistaken for a coin or a health potion. That is greyboxing, and it is what 2.3 did for the healing potion.
  4. Inspector → Add Component → Box Collider 2D. Decide whether Is Trigger is ticked before you leave this step, and be ready to defend the answer: a solid pair of boots is something you trip over, and your player already carries the Dynamic body a trigger pair needs.
  5. Inspector → Tag → the tag you made. Then Project window → drag the object out of the Hierarchy and into Assets/Prefabs: it is a prefab now, and the copy still standing in the cave is an instance of it.
  6. Scene view → move that instance somewhere a tester has to walk. Then Project window → Assets/Prefabs → drag Coin into the Hierarchy, and Scene view → put it on a shelf one jump cannot reach.
  7. Game view → press Play twice — once straight at the coin, once after collecting the pickup — and time how long a tester needs to work out what it is for. If you chose the potion, watch what happens when it runs out in mid-air, and write down what the player saw.
Test the whole loop, including death. Grab the pickup, then die on purpose. If your death rule from 2.2 reloads the scene, the Player is rebuilt from the prefab — so the maximum goes back to its Inspector value, and a potion's remaining seconds vanish with it. For the boots that is a real design question: is a permanent upgrade permanent for the run, or permanent for the save? Write down what you observe, then say which of the two has to change — the death rule, or where the fact lives.
In the Code ~30 min

This is the level-3 substitute for a walkthrough: the API is laid out below and the code is not. You write the file. Every row is a call or a declaration you have already typed in 6.2, 3.3 or 2.1 — read the cost column before you pick.

APIWhat you getWhat it costs
int maxJumps = 1; The ceiling you already declared in 6.2, and the one field this whole lesson changes. The refill and the walk-off charge both read it, so raising it is a one-line change — and it reaches both of them at once. Written once, in the class body. A second assignment somewhere else — in a pickup, in Start(), in a reload — is a second definition of the rule, and one of the two will eventually be wrong.
[SerializeField] private float doubleJumpDuration = 8f; The potion's dial: how many seconds of second jump a player buys. Only the temporary path needs it. [SerializeField] because it is a design number, exactly like jumpForce. A number in the Inspector is a promise you can tune without recompiling — and a decision you have to make. There is no correct value; there is only the one your cave was built for.
Time.deltaTime How long the last frame took, in seconds — the unit that turns a countdown into real time. You wrote this in 3.3 and the shape is identical: subtract while the number is above zero. Decrement by a whole number per frame and the potion lasts as long as your framerate says it does.
AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse) The flick from 4.5 and 6.1 — one instant change in momentum, which physics then spends over the following frames. Both jumps call the same method. It divides by mass, so retuning mass silently retunes both jumps.
OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) and other.CompareTag("Boots") The pickup callback and the tag check you have had since 2.1 — one branch more in a method that already handles the coin and the healing potion. It fires once per entry, and only if the tag exists in the project — which is why creating it is step two above.
other.gameObject and Destroy(Object) The whole object behind the collider you just touched, and the call that removes it at the end of the frame. Plain gameObject is you, and getting the two backwards destroys the player. Destroy(Object) is also deferred, so the object is alive for the rest of the frame.
Architectural specification: the ceiling.
  • What is maxJumps in a build where the player has picked up nothing? Say it out loud, then check that the field in the Inspector agrees with what you said.
  • Where is maxJumps written — how many lines, in how many methods? The refill in 6.2 reads it; does the pickup write it?
  • After the pickup, does jumpsRemaining get refilled immediately, or does the player wait until they land? Say which one you chose and what a tester feels.
Architectural specification: permanent or temporary.
  • State your choice, then state what the other one would have done to a level you have already built. "It is easier" is not an answer; "my cave has one gap I want the player to cross once and not again" is.
  • Temporary path: where does the remaining time live, what decrements it, and which comparison decides that the effect is over? Write the sentence before you write the line.
  • Temporary path: a player finishes the potion in mid-air with a jump unspent. What should happen to jumpsRemaining that frame, and which line does it without an error message?
  • Permanent path: the maximum is raised forever — forever what? Say which of your death rule, your scene load and your prefab rebuild can undo it, and whether you accept that.
Architectural specification: the pickup branch.
  • Which callback fires when the player touches it — the trigger one or the collision one? The answer depends on the collider setting you chose in the editor half, and it changes the parameter type you are handed.
  • How do you identify the pickup from inside that callback, and how do you reach the object that should disappear?
  • If you chose the potion: what happens if the player finds a second one while the first is still running? Add, replace, or clamp — pick one and say why.
  • What do you hand to Debug.Log(string message) so a tester can see the change with no UI in the game?

Deploy in neutral first. Write the pickup branch with no effect on the jump at all — destroy the object, log a line, change nothing. The player should play exactly as they did before. Turn the effect on only once that is true: a tag that fires is easier to find than a jump that does not.

Socratic: Choosing the Data

  1. Where does the jump allowance live — on the player, on the pickup, or on a manager? Your answer should sound like the one you gave in 2.1, and for the same reason.
  2. If you chose the potion, what is the type of "how much longer does this last", and what is its value a second after the player picks it up? If you chose the boots, what is the type of "do I have them", and where is that field after a death?
  3. Your walk-off rule from 6.2 charges one jump when you leave the ground without jumping. With the pickup in the game, is that still the rule you want — or does the second jump make it feel like a punishment? Say what the player experiences, not what the code does.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Say which field changed in 6.2's budget, and why nothing else had to
  • Explain why carrying boots off a ledge still leaves you one jump
  • Defend boots over potion, or potion over boots, in terms of a level you built
  • If temporary: say where the clock lives, what it counts in, and what happens the frame it runs out mid-air
  • If permanent: say what can undo it, and whether you accept that
  • Build a pickup end to end — tag, collider, effect — the way you built the healing potion
  • Design a soft gate: visible, unreachable, no damage, no text
  • Commit and push
